title: Coupling effect of nearest-neighbor interacting qubit chains to a single qubit system
authors: Manuel Allan L. Orongan, Lemuel John F. Sese, Rayda P. Gammag
abstract: This study establishes a theorem that provides sufficient criteria for identifying terms in any time-independent Hamiltonian that have no influence on local dynamics, local observables, or any local phenomena, without any approximation. The usefulness of this theorem is demonstrated by predicting the behavior of three systems. The first system consists of multiple qubit chains with Ising interactions. The second system is formed by a single qubit chain, differentiated by the substitution of Dzyalonshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction for the last Ising interaction. The predictions were verified by analytically deriving the reduced dynamics of both systems. A third system was also considered, namely, a short qubit chain with a transverse magnetic field on the intermediary environment qubit. This transverse magnetic field signals that the commutation relation required by our theorem no longer holds. The third system's local dynamics were also derived analytically, demonstrating that all Hamiltonian constituents contributed to the reduced dynamics. The physical consequences of our theorem's inapplicability were also explored using this third system by analyzing the entanglement dynamics between the qubits that do not directly interact. The results showed that the entanglement is caused by an \textit{emergent coupling} between the two non-directly interacting subsystems. This \textit{emergent coupling} arises from the non-commutativity of the intermediate interactions connecting the two subsystems. When searching for these \textit{emergent couplings}, our theorem can eliminate intermediate interactions that will not produce them.
summary: This paper develops a theorem defining when certain parts of a system's Hamiltonian are inert regarding local dynamics. By testing this theorem against various qubit chain models, the authors show that violating the required commutation relations allows for an 'emergent coupling.' This emergent coupling can generate measurable entanglement between subsystems that do not interact directly in the original Hamiltonian.
main_problem: The study aims to establish a rigorous theorem identifying Hamiltonian terms that do not influence local dynamics or observables, while also exploring cases where this assumption breaks down.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that when specific commutation relations are violated (e.g., by applying a transverse field), non-local interactions can generate an 'emergent coupling' leading to measurable entanglement between previously uncoupled subsystems.
method: The analysis involves deriving the reduced density matrix using partial tracing over environment degrees of freedom, comparing results derived under strict commutation conditions versus those where they fail.
model_or_system: The models involve coupled qubit chains (Ising interactions) interacting with a central local qubit. The system is analyzed by varying coupling strengths and external fields to test the limits of the theoretical theorem.
key_observables: Reduced density matrix ($\hat{ho}_0(t)$), Concurrence ($C(\hat{ho}_{02})$) for entanglement measurement.
important_parameters: Transverse magnetic field strength ($\omega_1$), coupling strengths ($G_{ij}$), and the ratio of these parameters relative to each other.
main_assumptions: The initial theorem relies on specific commutation relations $[\hat{H}, \hat{H}_{E2}] = 0$; the entanglement analysis assumes initial unbiased probability amplitudes for certain states.
figures_summary: Figure 4 illustrates the time-evolution of concurrence, showing that significant entanglement generation occurs when the transverse field ($\omega_1$) is comparable in magnitude to the primary coupling strengths ($G_{ij}$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes a theorem for local dynamics independence based on commutation relations. It then tests this with multiple qubit chains (confirming the theorem) and subsequently analyzes a third system where breaking the commutation relation leads to emergent, non-local entanglement.
why_interesting: This work provides deep insight into how seemingly irrelevant Hamiltonian terms can become dynamically relevant through non-commuting interactions, which is crucial for understanding decoherence and information flow in complex quantum systems.
